metadata.file_name: Hernández-Ramos & Araya. (2025). Do School Activities Foster Creative Thinking? An Analysis of PISA Results.pdf
metadata.title: Do School Activities Foster Creative Thinking? An Analysis of PISA Results

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 creative thinking outcomes and PISA 2018/2022 reading (and other domain) scores aggregated at the country/economy level (64–80 records depending on the input), after excluding economies with sampling-standard issues. The manuscript does not report applying PISA student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or any replicate-weight variance estimation, and it instead relies on descriptive correlations and ordinary least squares regression on country-level means. Because the analysis is not described as a complex-survey estimation procedure, the results should be interpreted as associations among country aggregates rather than population-representative estimates. For analysts replicating with microdata, appropriate PISA complex-sample weights and plausible-value procedures would be required for student-level achievement, but this paper’s design uses published/aggregated scores and does not document weight usage.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not describe any missing-data strategy for the country/economy records used in the correlations and regressions (e.g., how missing questionnaire percentages or missing domain scores were handled beyond excluding records with missing sampling standards and requiring all input fields). Because the dependent variables are country-level mean creative thinking scores and domain scores derived from PISA 2022, plausible values are not handled explicitly at the student level; the study effectively works with aggregated scores. This omission is a reporting gap because the reader cannot verify whether missing components were listwise excluded, imputed, or otherwise treated before computing the country means.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2022 creative thinking data and related PISA 2018/2022 domain scores, but the analytic dataset is country/economy-level (64 records for creative thinking means and domain snapshots; 74 records for weekly participation percentages; 78–80 records for PISA 2018/2022 domain scores). Excluded records where one or more PISA sampling standards were missing or flagged with caution, and retained only records containing all required input fields (creative thinking mean, four creative thinking domain scores, weekly participation percentages for the specified activities, and the relevant PISA 2018/2022 reading/mathematics/science scores). Additionally, for RQ1–RQ3 analyses, excluded specific economies due to sampling-standard differences: Australia, Canada, Denmark, Hong Kong, Ireland, Jamaica, Latvia, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Panama, and the United Kingdom, resulting in 54 OECD countries and associated economies.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (country mean; four domains aggregated to overall mean score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pearson correlations (Table 1): programming −0.578 (p<0.001), creative writing −0.700 (p<0.001), science club −0.810 (p<0.001), drama/theatre −0.802 (p<0.001), debate −0.841 (p<0.001), publications −0.868 (p<0.001); PCA-derived composite correlations (Table 4): Var 1 −0.852 (p<0.001), Var 2 −0.129 (ns). Regression (Table 5–6): Model 1 R=0.852, adjusted R²=0.721; Var 1 Beta=−0.852, t=−11.736, p=0.000. Model 2 R=0.881, adjusted R²=0.768; Var 1 Beta=−0.949, t=−13.180, p=0.000; Var 2 Beta=0.245, t=3.409, p=0.001. Programming excluded as non-significant (p=0.604 in Model 1; p=0.448 in Model 2).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking country-mean the study leveraged Var 1 (writing/critical activities), Var 2 (art/music activities), and programming activity frequency to explain the creative thinking mean score, finding that Var 1 had a strong negative association (Beta=−0.949) while Var 2 had a small positive association (Beta=0.245) and programming was not significant. This indicates that simply increasing participation in certain school activities may not translate into higher PISA-measured creative thinking unless the pedagogical design aligns with the creative-thinking processes assessed by PISA, though causality cannot be inferred from these country-level associations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (Scientific Problem Solving domain; country mean)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Pearson correlations (Table 8): science club −0.666 (p<0.001), programming −0.438 (p=0.001). Scatterplot regressions: science club vs domain y=−0.7794x+38.333, R²=0.4438; programming vs domain y=−0.4668x+36.509, R²=0.1916.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking country-mean data for the scientific problem-solving domain, the study leveraged science club participation frequency and programming activity frequency to explain domain performance, finding significant negative associations for both predictors (science club r=−0.666; programming r=−0.438). This indicates that the way science clubs and programming are implemented may be misaligned with the open-ended, idea-generating processes required by the PISA scientific problem-solving tasks, though the evidence remains correlational at the country level.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (Scientific Problem Solving domain; country mean)
main_findings.target_variable: Scientific problem-solving domain score predicted from PISA 2018/2022 reading
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression summary (Table 11, PISA 2018 scientific domain): Model 1 R=0.870, adjusted R²=0.751 (reading 2018 only). Regression summary (Table 12, PISA 2022 scientific domain): Model 1 R=0.884, adjusted R²=0.777 (reading 2022 only). Mathematics and science scores excluded as non-significant in the described models (per text; Tables S11–S12).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking country-mean data for the scientific problem-solving domain, the study leveraged reading scores from PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 to predict domain performance, finding strong positive associations in both years (adjusted R²=0.751 and 0.777, respectively). This indicates that reading literacy is a foundational skill for scientific problem-solving as assessed by PISA, implying that cross-curricular literacy supports may improve performance in creative scientific tasks, though the study remains correlational.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (country mean; overall creative thinking score)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking mean score predicted from PISA 2018/2022 reading and other domain scores
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression summary (Table 9, PISA 2018): Model 1 R=0.912, adjusted R²=0.829 (reading 2018 only). Model 2 R=0.929, adjusted R²=0.857 (reading 2018 + Var 1); mathematics and science 2018 and other variables excluded as non-significant (per text; coefficients in Table S9).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking country-mean data with PISA 2018 domain scores as predictors, the study leveraged PISA 2018 reading score and Var 1 to explain creative thinking performance, finding that reading 2018 was the strongest positive predictor (adjusted R²=0.829) and that adding Var 1 improved fit (adjusted R²=0.857). This indicates that reading comprehension is closely linked to the creative-thinking processes measured by PISA, suggesting that literacy-focused instructional practices may be a prerequisite for improving creative thinking, though the analysis does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (country mean; overall creative thinking score)
main_findings.target_variable: Creative thinking mean score predicted from PISA 2022 reading and other domain scores
main_findings.performance_metrics: Regression summary (Table 10, PISA 2022): Model 1 R=0.941, adjusted R²=0.883 (reading 2022 only). Model 2 R=0.950, adjusted R²=0.898 (reading 2022 + programming). Mathematics and science 2022 excluded as non-significant (per text; coefficients in Table S10).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking country-mean data with PISA 2022 domain scores as predictors, the study leveraged PISA 2022 reading score and programming activity frequency to explain creative thinking performance, finding that reading 2022 was a strong positive predictor (adjusted R²=0.883) and that programming contributed additional explanatory power in the multivariable model (adjusted R²=0.898). This indicates that strengthening reading proficiency may be central to improving PISA-measured creative thinking, while programming’s role appears limited and context-dependent, and causality cannot be inferred from these correlational regressions.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes associations between students’ participation in school activities and PISA 2022 creative thinking outcomes, using country/economy-level records derived from PISA 2022 creative thinking means and its four domains (written, visual, social problem solving, scientific problem solving), plus PISA 2018 and PISA 2022 reading/mathematics/science scores. The analytic sample is 54 OECD countries and associated economies after excluding economies with sampling-standard issues; the paper does not report student-level modeling or complex-survey estimation. The strongest relationships are descriptive and regression-based: for overall creative thinking, Var 1 (writing/critical activities) shows a strong negative association (adjusted R²=0.721 in Model 1; adjusted R²=0.768 in Model 2), while reading scores are the most consistent positive predictors (adjusted R²=0.829 for PISA 2018 reading; 0.883 for PISA 2022 reading). For the scientific problem-solving domain, science club and programming participation are negatively correlated (r=−0.666 and r=−0.438). Limitations include the absence of documented plausible-value/missing-data procedures at the student level and the correlational, country-aggregate design, so causality cannot be inferred.
